todays_goal: Math is the required review subject: repair distributive-property execution before combining like terms. Advance History to Macedon after a one-line Sparta correction; advance Science to corrective lenses after fixing the retina misconception; advance French to futur proche; extend TacticLab into Coach Mode; continue The Westing Game AR reading; advance Literature to multiple-clue inference; and write a camera-vs-eye compare/contrast explanation.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Distributive Mastery and Combining Like Terms
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed strong percent accuracy and conceptual understanding of distribution, but Atticus inconsistently multiplied the outside factor by every term. He also still dropped the negative sign when naming signed terms.
lessons.course_context: Math is today's required review subject. Repair the exact distributive-property gap first, then introduce combining like terms only after a 5/5 repair gate.
learning_objectives: Apply the distributive property to every term inside parentheses.
Identify signed terms accurately.
Distinguish equation from expression by the equals sign.
Combine like terms.
Check equivalent expressions with substitution when useful.
lessons.why_it_matters: These are core Grade 6 algebra skills and the foundation for simplifying expressions and solving equations.

vocabulary.definition: terms with the same variable part
different-looking expressions with the same value
multiply the outside factor by every term inside parentheses

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: Friday showed that you know what distribution means, but you sometimes multiplied only the first term. Today, every term must get multiplied. Pass the 5/5 repair gate first. Then learn to combine like terms.

worked_examples.title: Multiple coefficient
worked_examples.explanation: The outside 5 multiplies the whole term 2x and the 3.

worked_examples.title: Combine like terms
worked_examples.explanation: 3x and 2x are like terms; 4 is not.

guided_practice.prompt: How can you tell an equation from an expression?

independent_practice.prompt: Simplify 5x+3x.
Simplify 6y+2+y.
Simplify 4a+5+3a+2.
Rewrite and simplify 3(x+4)+2x.
Rewrite and simplify 2(3y+5)+y.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Be concise and demanding but supportive. Begin with the exact Friday misses. Use the whiteboard to draw arrows from the outside factor to EVERY term using examples different from the assigned questions. Do not give an assigned answer. If he multiplies only the first term, say only: 'Check whether the outside number reached every term.' Require a retry. Do not advance to like terms until the 5/5 repair gate is passed.
lessons.teacher_notes: Review subject for Day 19. Hold new algebra until repair gate passes.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.lesson_title: After the Peloponnesian War: The Rise of Macedon
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed solid understanding of the end of the Peloponnesian War, but Atticus briefly reversed Sparta's adaptation. Sparta was strongest on land and built stronger naval power to challenge Athens at sea.
lessons.course_context: Move from the end of the Peloponnesian War to the weakened Greek city-state system and the rise of Macedon under Philip II.
learning_objectives: Correctly explain Sparta's land-to-sea adaptation.
Explain why continued Greek rivalry created an opening for Macedon.
Locate Macedon relative to the Greek city-states.
Explain why Chaeronea changed the balance of power.
lessons.why_it_matters: This explains how a divided Greek world came under Macedonian dominance and sets up Alexander the Great.

vocabulary.definition: a kingdom north of the major Greek city-states
the Macedonian king who built a powerful army and expanded Macedonian control
the 338 BCE battle in which Philip defeated a major Greek alliance

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: the Peloponnesian War ended, but fighting among Greek states continued. That weakened the Greek world while Macedon grew stronger under Philip II.

worked_examples.title: Cause chain
worked_examples.problem: How did Greek rivalry help Macedon?
worked_examples.solution: long wars -> continued rivalry -> weakened city-states -> stronger Macedon -> Chaeronea
worked_examples.explanation: A divided region was easier for a growing outside power to dominate.

independent_practice.prompt: Why did the end of the Peloponnesian War not create lasting peace?
How could years of war make the Greek city-states easier to challenge?
Where was Macedon compared with the major Greek city-states?
What made Philip II powerful?
Why was Chaeronea important?

exit_ticket.prompt: In 4-5 sentences, explain how fighting among Greek city-states helped create an opening for Macedon.
exit_ticket.answer: Mention long wars/rivalry, weakened city-states, Macedon's growth under Philip II, and Macedonian victory at Chaeronea.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach before questioning. Start with one short correction: Sparta was a land power that built stronger naval power. Then use the whiteboard for a simple north-to-south sketch with Macedon above the Greek city-states and a five-link cause chain. Keep wording age-appropriate. Do not answer assigned questions.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance to Macedon after one strategy correction.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: Corrective Lenses: Helping Light Reach the Retina
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed solid camera/eye comparison. One repair remains: the retina detects light and sends signals; it does not make the image clear.
lessons.course_context: Use the lens/refraction model to explain nearsightedness, farsightedness, and corrective lenses.
learning_objectives: State the retina's actual job.
Explain where light focuses in nearsightedness and farsightedness.
Explain how concave and convex corrective lenses change incoming light.
lessons.why_it_matters: This applies the same refraction model to a real technology many people use every day.

vocabulary.definition: nearsightedness; distant objects are blurry because light focuses too soon
farsightedness; nearby objects may be blurry because light would focus too far back
a lens that changes incoming light so the eye can focus it more accurately

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: the retina detects light and sends signals. Corrective lenses do their work before the light reaches the retina. Concave lenses spread rays; convex lenses bend rays inward.

worked_examples.title: Myopia
worked_examples.problem: Light focuses in front of the retina.
worked_examples.solution: Use a concave lens to spread rays slightly.
worked_examples.explanation: The final focus moves back toward the retina.

worked_examples.title: Hyperopia
worked_examples.problem: Light would focus behind the retina.
worked_examples.solution: Use a convex lens to start bending rays inward.
worked_examples.explanation: The final focus moves forward toward the retina.

independent_practice.prompt: What must happen for an image to look sharp to the eye?
What does the retina actually do?
In nearsightedness, does light focus in front of or behind the retina?
Which lens helps nearsightedness?
Which lens helps farsightedness?

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain how corrective lenses change light before it reaches the eye.
exit_ticket.answer: They refract incoming light so the eye's optics can focus it closer to the retina.

exit_ticket.prompt: What is one difference between the job of the retina and the job of a corrective lens?
exit_ticket.answer: A corrective lens changes the direction of light; the retina detects light and sends signals to the brain.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach first. Correct the retina misconception in one sentence. On the whiteboard, draw a retina line, then one focus in front and one behind it. Add a concave or convex lens to show the correction. Use examples different from the assigned questions. Never reveal assigned answers.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed correct use of je vais, tu vas, nous allons, and ils vont. Negative possession is substantially secure.
lessons.course_context: Use aller as an auxiliary to express what someone is going to do.
learning_objectives: Retrieve common forms of aller.
Build aller + infinitive near-future sentences.
Produce simple true near-future sentences orally and in writing.
lessons.why_it_matters: The near future is one of the most useful structures in everyday French.

vocabulary.definition: the base form of a verb, such as jouer, lire, or manger

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: say je vais, tu vas, nous allons, ils vont. Then add an infinitive: Je vais jouer. Nous allons manger.

worked_examples.title: Nous
worked_examples.problem: We are going to play football.

independent_practice.prompt: Je ____ jouer. (aller)
Nous ____ manger. (aller)
Translate: They are going to watch the match.
Translate: You are going to read. (tu)
Write one true sentence about something you are going to do today.

exit_ticket.prompt: Say one sentence with je vais + verb and one with nous allons + verb.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep French oral and concise. Begin with four aller forms. Model natural pronunciation, then require Atticus to speak before writing. Do not over-explain grammar. For an assigned item, cue the form but do not give the full answer.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance from present aller to futur proche.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.unit_title: Creative Technology and AI Builder Lab
lessons.previous_learning: TacticLab introduced formations, player placement, drag-and-drop, and lineup state. Monday extends it into visible tactical behavior.
lessons.course_context: Add interactive team-tactics controls and require each control to visibly affect pitch state or the tactics summary.
learning_objectives: Create team-width, defensive-line, attack-style, and pressing controls.
Connect controls to visible on-pitch behavior.
Persist tactics state.
Test and repair interactive behavior using acceptance criteria.
lessons.why_it_matters: This builds real product skill: state, interaction design, visible cause/effect, persistence, testing, and iterative vibe coding.

vocabulary.definition: the current selected value of an interface control
a visible change calculated from the current settings

lessons.written_instruction: Laptop only. Build Coach Mode so tactical choices visibly change spacing, defensive line, attacking arrows/support, and the tactics summary.

worked_examples.title: Width flow
worked_examples.problem: What should happen when width changes from Balanced to Wide?
worked_examples.solution: Update width state -> move players farther apart horizontally -> update tactics summary.
worked_examples.explanation: A control is meaningful only if the product visibly responds.

guided_practice.prompt: Whiteboard the controls and the state flow before building.

independent_practice.prompt: Add Width: Narrow/Balanced/Wide.
Add Defensive Line: Deep/Balanced/High.
Add Attack Style: Possession/Balanced/Direct.
Add Pressing: Low/Medium/High.
Make each setting visibly affect the pitch or tactics summary.
Test Save Tactics and Reset Tactics.

exit_ticket.prompt: Demo one tactical control, show the visible change, and explain what state the app remembers.
exit_ticket.answer: Any functioning control with visible derived behavior and persisted settings.

lessons.voice_prompt: Laptop only. Be a concise product coach, not a lecturer. Use the whiteboard to map controls -> state -> visible pitch change -> summary -> save. Ask one product question at a time. Do not teach syntax unless asked. Do not take over the build. When a feature fails, require EXPECTED / ACTUAL / STEPS / RETEST.
lessons.teacher_notes: Practical builder emphasis. No paper Q&A.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed major improvement: Atticus correctly distinguished inference from plot summary and guess, and supported theme with textual clues.
lessons.course_context: Advance from one-clue inference to stronger inferences supported by multiple clues.
learning_objectives: Use two clues to support one inference.
Explain how multiple clues strengthen a conclusion.
Use multiple clues to support theme.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong close reading requires weighing several details rather than relying on a single line.

vocabulary.definition: a conclusion supported by more than one detail

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: Friday proved you understand inference. Today, use two or more clues that point in the same direction. Do not force a clue if it does not fit.

worked_examples.title: Nervous
worked_examples.problem: Noah waits outside and repeatedly wipes his hands on his jeans.
worked_examples.explanation: Two separate details support the same inference.

independent_practice.prompt: What two clues show Rina learned from the first test?
Why does Rina make the second tower shorter?
What can you infer from the fact that she does not smile when another tower leans?
What does the final sentence reveal about how her thinking changed?
Write a theme and support it with two clues.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why is an inference supported by two clues often stronger than one supported by only one?
exit_ticket.answer: More independent evidence makes the conclusion better supported.

lessons.voice_prompt: Friday was successful, so raise the bar. Keep questions plain. Require two clues when asked. If Atticus gives plot only, ask: 'What does that tell you?' If he gives an inference without evidence, ask: 'Which two clues support that?' Do not supply the inference.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.lesson_title: Compare and Explain: Camera vs Eye
lessons.previous_learning: Friday's evidence-to-inference paragraph was strong: clear claim, two details, reasoning, and conclusion.
lessons.course_context: Advance to compare/contrast explanatory writing using science content.
learning_objectives: State accurate similarities and differences.
Explain why one difference matters.
Use science vocabulary accurately.
Maintain complete sentence boundaries.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong academic writing connects content knowledge to clear explanation.

vocabulary.definition: explain how things are alike and different

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: compare a camera and an eye. Give at least one similarity and one difference. Then explain why one difference matters.

worked_examples.title: Camera vs eye
worked_examples.solution: Both detect light, but a camera sensor records electronic image data while the retina sends neural signals to the brain.
worked_examples.explanation: The difference matters because vision depends on brain interpretation.

independent_practice.prompt: Write 6-7 sentences: How is a camera like an eye, and how is it different? Include at least two similarities/differences and explain why one difference matters.

exit_ticket.answer: Accurate similarity, accurate difference, significance, correct vocabulary, checked sentence endings.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not dictate sentences. Ask one short planning question at a time: What is one similarity? What is one difference? Why does that difference matter? Correct science facts before accepting them, but make Atticus produce the wording.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance from narrative-text evidence writing to content-based explanation.
